utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Now we continue from where we stopped yesterday. Can you remind the witness he is still on his oath? Let's have the appearances first and then we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Teresa McHenry for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The witness apparently has problems with the earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath. I wish to remind you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I wish to remind you that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Teresa McHenry with the Office of the Prosecutor. I appear here with Mr. Giuliano Turone, my co-counsel, and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, defence counsel of Mr. Zdravko Mucic. With me as co-counsel is Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, lawyer from Sarajevo. I am defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I appear here on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Ms. Cynthia McMurrey from the United States. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, I think you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If your Honours would like, I can give you an update from my discussions with the witness yesterday before Mr. Ackerman starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That's ideal. Let's hear your discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: First of all, your Honour, it is the case that in a published book entitled "Suffering of the Serbs in Konjic and Tarcin" this witness' statement, which is in Serbo-Croatian and is about half a page, is found. I will note that the defence was advised that in last year or in January that there were many books that were publicly available about the suffering -- about what happened in Celebici, and in particular then in a court filing on 16th January 1997 the Prosecution again reported in response to a motion filed by the Defence, a general motion for disclosure of exculpatory evidence, among other things -- the Prosecution noted that it was aware of two books in particular, which included this book, "Suffering of Serbs in Konjic and Tarcin", edited by Dusica Bojic in Belgrade, from the Commissariat for the Refugees of the Republic of Serbia, 1995. So the Defence was told this book was published and was available. Although it was stated it was not necessary, the Prosecution did not believe it was necessary, the Prosecution reported in this motion filed before the court that it was willing to permit inspection of these books. So the witness has indicated -- has now seen this book and indicated that this statement is, in fact, the statement that he is referring to. It does not appear that this is the exact same book that he saw, and I will note that this is a book in which certain things such as the introduction I think are in English and only the -- and certain witness statements, some of which are named and some of which are not, are in Serbo-Croatian. So it may be that this witness has seen an earlier version of this book that was just in Serbo-Croatian. This witness does remember -- indicates that he remembers the editor of the book that he saw, and that book was edited by Sretan Jakouljevic, who is also in Belgrade. So this book is presumably available in book stores or libraries. So this witness also agreed to contact -- try to contact the person who he believes has a copy of the exact book he saw, but he cannot do that now. The Prosecution believes, given that the Defence may look at this one and has been able to look at it since January of 1997, it's not necessary for this witness to continue any further efforts, but I will just update the court that that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It depends on what the Defence regards the statement which hasn't been tendered to them made by the witness, but even in that case, except the witness is in possession of the statements, there is no way he can tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. This raises another issue and maybe the Prosecution can help us with this. Under the provisions of Rule 66(A) it requires the Prosecutor to provide the Defence, even without request, copies of all statements of witnesses in the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: In their possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's correct, your Honour. I would like to know if there are other prosecution witnesses whose statements are in this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, read Rule 66A: "Statements obtained by the Prosecutor".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand it, there is a decision, and I think it is in the Tadic case, but I could be wrong -- it may be in the Blaskic case -- which says it doesn't make any difference how these statements come into the possession of OTP. It defines "obtained" in a broad way that "obtained" means get as opposed to questioning the witness, but I could be wrong on that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you exercised your entitlement under Rule 67B? I think you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Although we did ask for request under 66B, it would be my position that Rule 66A is a requirement on the Prosecution, whether or not the Defence asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that. That is what you should attach to the indictment and the like, but with the exercise that arises under 66B, then you could have gone through all the documents which they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We did, of course, file a 66B motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So you could have gone through that and found whatever they had and if this is one of the things which you have gone through, I think that might have satisfied the provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The only other thing I would suggest to the court would be this: several witnesses have been asked: "Did you give statements to anybody else or did you talk to anybody else?" If those statements -- if there are statements from those witnesses that are contained in that book, arguably that would be Rule 68, exculpatory material, as it may affect the credibility of prosecution witnesses or prosecution evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That depends if it is exculpatory. It is not merely if someone spoke or wrote a letter to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. What I have in mind is if someone says "I did not make any other statement" and there is another statement, that goes right to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we are even expanding the meaning of "statement" too much, as if what anybody said to anybody, to any family friend, is a statement with respect to what we are going through. It's not necessarily so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear what you intend to put in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult for me to respond to what the Prosecutor has just told us unless I can see the document that she was holding there, and I would like to have an opportunity to take a look at that time for just a moment, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Surely, but as Miss McHenry is saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As Ms. McHenry has said, the Prosecution indicated to you these two books in at least January 1997. Why don't you look at those -- why don't you accept it from her and go through the book and see what the statements contained in that book were?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Until Ms. McHenry made that statement this morning I had no idea they had filed such a document. It was just one of the things I have not yet got around to reading in this case. So my colleagues may have been fully aware of that. I was not. I admit should have been. I guess what disturbs me at this point is in connection with several witnesses that have testified since I have arrived here, either me or one or more of my colleagues have enquired of them whether they have made any other formal written statements to an organisation such as the Association of Detainees, and many of them have denied having done so. I think on more than one occasion since I have been here the Prosecutor has been asked to state to the court whether or not they had knowledge of any other statements given by such witnesses to the Association of Detainees or any other organisation, and my recollection is that on each occasion the Prosecutor has told the court that they had no knowledge of any other statements given by the witness, and had no knowledge that any statements had been given to an organisation such as the Association of Detainees. Now I am not capable of making more than that kind of broad general statement at this point because I have not seen the book. If the only witness whose statement appears in that book is the one seated before us today, then I have very little to complain about, because they have brought now today to our attention that that statement exists in that book. In terms of my further cross-examination of this witness, I think it's important that I be provided with at least a copy of that portion of the book which contains the statement that he made, so that I can make a determination whether there is any material in it that I might be able to use for impeachment purposes. So that's kind of where I stand with regard to that right now. I must say that I'm -- I was surprised this morning -- maybe some of my colleagues were not -- to learn of the existence of such a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose it depends largely on the extent of researches into what has happened since then, because if counsel has been very conversant with what has been going on, they might have known about the existence of the books, irrespective of whether the Prosecution knew of it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not -- is happy to give a copy -- to let the Defence counsel use this book during his cross-examination. I will tell defence counsel that it is only in Serbo-Croatian and we do not have a translation, but possibly co-counsel who is there -- I also just want to clarify the record. I believe what the Prosecution has stated is that any statements that it has received from the Association, that the Prosecution has received,, have been given. It may well be that certain witnesses have given other statements, be they to the media, government agencies and things like that that we just don't know. So please do not take anything the Prosecution has said to state there were no other statements made. I believe what we stated was that the Association had not provided us any statements that we had not turned over to the Defence, just so that's clear. I'm happy to let Defence counsel use this book or maybe I can -- a copy can be made later on, if you request also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, since it is in Serbo-Croatian there's very little use I can make of it right at the moment. I would ask leave to have it made available during the next break so that I can have someone look at it for me and tell me what this statement says. I see the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution a translation of that statement in?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. In all frankness it was only -- I don't know that we were even aware that this statement was in there but after this issue came up yesterday, we found it. So we do not have a translation. I did quickly have someone look at it this morning and give me a brief summary but we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does his name occur in this book?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What protection can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You will be the first person to translate the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Your Honours, the first thing I notice as I look at this is this seems to be a regularly published book, not some kind of a private publication. It appears to be a book that might be available in book stores, libraries, things of that nature; in other words, a public document. The other thing I notice is that this witness' name appears publicly in this book without the protection that has been requested here in this court. I don't know if that's significant or not, but that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just speak to that? It is the case that with a number of witnesses the protection they request is that they are testifying here as witnesses, not that they were victims of Celebici camp and, for instance, there are a number of witnesses whose name appears in the indictment, who nonetheless have requested protection, and what they are seeking is not protection from what happened to them in Celebici or their identities, but their status as a witness. So the fact that there is a book in which it is made public that they are a witness in Celebici -- a victim in Celebici, the Prosecution does not believe would mean they are not entitled to protection. It is the case -- it is the Prosecution's understanding that this book is available. In fact, in our January filing in which we mentioned several books, we indicated that both of them are books that are publicly -- as far as we know are publicly available, and we consider them public material rather than statements or anything like that. Maybe it would be best if I can have -- I will request that someone from the Prosecution office come in and get this and I'll make copies of the witness' statement so that all Defence counsel may have them during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's fine. I would -- I guess I'm about to have a conversation with Ms. McHenry that doesn't need to take place on the record. I'll have that conversation during the break. In any event, I am prepared to go forward with my cross-examination excluding anything I might want to do with regard to this book, and if I finish my cross-examination prior to our morning break, then I would ask leave to have this witness brought back for additional cross-examination after I've had a chance to look at the statement if I think it's appropriate; otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That's all right, because if you really want to impeach him you could not do so until you have seen what the statement is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So you can continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. M, I would like to talk to you a bit more about the memoires that you have written regarding your experiences; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to have you tell us if in connection with writing those memoires that you focused primarily or exclusively on your experiences in Celebici camp and in Musala, or if it went broader into all of your experiences prior to and during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you recall, I said that the memoires were something I was writing for myself, something that I do not wish to publish at least for the time being, and to satisfy your curiosity I will tell you that I'm covering the period from 1992, that is before the outbreak of the conflict, until the end. I just mentioned this by chance, that I was writing these memoires. I said that I didn't know whether they would ever be published. If they are, they will be available. I'm talking about my experiences and all the events that happened from January 1992 to the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you base these writings strictly on your own memory and your own experiences, or did you conduct some additional research and use additional materials to help you in writing these memoires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They have to do with my personal experiences, my personal reflections about the situation, about the war itself. I didn't use any other material. Memoires are memoires.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Prior to May of 1992 you, of course, had learned a great deal about what was going on in the former Yugoslavia and specifically in Bosnia, had you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the mass media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And from discussions with other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You learned a great deal about what was going on by watching television, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that primarily was the television from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was Sarajevo television, because I was living in the environs of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did there not come a time when you could no longer receive the Sarajevo television but only the Belgrade television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time I could not watch television, because there was no electricity. We couldn't watch television at all. Electricity was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it things that you had learned from television that made it clear to you that it might be a good idea for you to arm yourselves, the citizens of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that I was watching Sarajevo television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you watching television from TV Srna, from the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the official TV Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was it that occurred prior to your acquiring a weapon and other Serbs in Bradina acquiring weapons that caused you to believe that that might be necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The political situation itself in the Republic, especially the political situation in the municipality of Konjic, where the Serb population held less than 20 per cent of the share, total share of the population. I don't know the exact figure. The people who were fleeing from the town of Konjic and from other parts where they were in the minority, so that even before the attack on Bradina itself, people were intimidated where they were in the minority. They fled from town. They came to Bradina. They fled to Sarajevo, fearing the worst, and learning from this experience of others, I had a dilemma whether I should take my wife and children away from Bradina or whether I should stay. Thus believing that a conflict could break out, I stayed. At least I didn't believe the war could occur in the way it did and that is why I stayed; otherwise I would have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you knew about the various speeches and statements being made by Slobodan Milosevic regarding his ideas about creating a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am familiar with that idea, but I personally did not support such an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Prior to the problems that developed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992, there had been, had there not, what might be described as a peaceful co-existence among the peoples who inhabited that region regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that before the conflict I was one of the organisers who tried to find people of goodwill who were willing to negotiate with the villages in which the Muslims were in the majority, and I formed such a committee, and I said yesterday that I went three times to three different villages to try and find ways of avoiding an armed conflict, to try and find a solution at least in our part of the country so that the tensions would be eased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Prior to all these difficulties in the late 1980s, the people living in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the area where you lived were enjoying a pretty good standard of living, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was very much a European standard of living. You had automobiles, telephones, television, a good society to live in; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to respectfully object. I have not objected up to now but I am going to object as to relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I think the relevancy of this was established by the Prosecution when they called Ms. Calic. I am simply exploring many of the issues she testified about. I think the Prosecution has made it relevant to the court by calling Miss Calic that the Tribunal cannot really understand the ramifications of this case without understanding the background of the conflict and that's what I'm pursuing and I think it's totally appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, but this witness did not give any evidence to that. What I thought you were pursuing was the fact of the question you asked. What made him decide to arm himself? I think that was what you were pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course that's what I'm pursuing and that's what I'm trying to get to, yes. Did you ever become -- I'm not sure you answered my last question and that was with regard to the standard of living that you had. It was a good standard of living prior to the outbreak of these problems, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relatively speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did there come a time before the residents of Bradina decided to arm themselves that you became aware, for instance, of the events that had been occurring in the Krajina region of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said since about February of 1992 we had no possibility of watching television because the electricity had been cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever learn about the activities, for instance of a man named Milan Babic in Knin in the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew, of course, that at some point Bradina became a pretty strategic location with regard to the war that had broken out in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Strategic? I can say that Bradina was a place where people organised themselves. There was no organisation from outside. The people organised within so that they would try in a peaceful way to preserve peace. They tried that, but it was -- they organised it -- they organised themselves in order to try to protect their homes and their mothers and wives. There was no strategic importance for anybody but ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You, of course, understand that Bradina was located on the main highway and the main railroad from Sarajevo to the coast, to the Adriatic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do know that in April of 1992 Sarajevo was placed under siege and shelling began of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that there were problems in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you knew that Sarajevo was under siege and the problem of simple supply --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know what ... no, I did not know that. I don't know what siege you are referring to, not even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know that Sarajevo was fired upon by Serb artillery almost daily for more than two years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a war going on in Sarajevo and that there was shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that the United Nations was trying to keep the airport in Sarajevo open so that the citizens of Sarajevo could be supplied with food and medicine and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't understand the question. May I ask what period of time you are referring to, because I have to remind you that I was arrested in May of 1992 and I was in the Celebici camp, and I don't think that whatever you've mentioned here in Sarajevo and the siege and the attempts of the UN to provide food and medicine, all this was happening following that, so I'm not familiar with any of these events that you're referring to, because I was in prison at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you do know this: you do know that Bradina had tunnels on both sides of Bradina that could be used very effectively to close off both the railroad and the highway simply by bombing those tunnels? You knew that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that and this was done. Tunnels were closed off on both sides. From the side of Konjic I know the person's name, the person who did it. I can tell that. On the other side it was also closed by putting there earth. So we had no opportunity -- we had no possibility of going either in the direction of Sarajevo or in the direction of Konjic from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew, of course, did you not, that it was a major interest of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time to try to keep that road open so that Sarajevo could be supplied with food, medicines, things of that nature; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that. I also don't know if you know, because I personally was on one of these barricades, and except for a search of the passengers who were passing through, and between the two attacks on Bradina, people who were passing through from Konjic who needed medical help in Sarajevo, they were let through, and they were going to Sarajevo and coming back. So the territory through Bradina was not blocked, but there was a ramp, and with the regular security measures, the control. So the road through Bradina was never blocked in the sense of 100 per cent blockade. There were checkpoints for security reasons, for fear of weapons coming through and for fear of attack, of sabotage attacks. Throughout this period the road was open and passage was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew, did you not, that the interests involved there were the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to keep the road open to supply Sarajevo, and the Bosnian Serb Army wanted to keep the road closed in order to cut off Sarajevo. You knew that was the main mission of both sides of the conflict at that point; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what either side wanted. I know that the army of the Republika Srpska had not put a blockade in Bradina. These were people, local people who had organised themselves, and there were people who were fleeing to Bradina. Based on their bad experiences, people wanted to protect themselves. There were no orders on the Republika Srpska army. We were organised ourselves. We organised self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you know, do you not, that the reason that Bradina was attacked was an effort to keep the road open, that that was what the purpose of that attack was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm surprised you are asking so many policing questions which this witness will not be able to answer. These are things which go into the control of the areas. He has given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he doesn't know the answers, he is perfectly free to say he doesn't know and I will go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So there's no point. If he may not know, why ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You recall my last question. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When the battle of Bradina started you told us that you were manning your position with an automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And shots were being fired on both sides; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the wider area of Bradina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you actually fired your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A number of times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that when it became clear to you that the forces trying to defend Bradina were seriously out numbered and that you should surrender, you surrendered, carrying with you a weapon that it was obvious had been fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Following that surrender, and I'm just going to go very briefly over this, because it has been largely covered, immediately following the surrender, prior to your being loaded on trucks, you've told us that you were beaten rather severely over a fairly long period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, as a result of that beating, you were bleeding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your arm was severely injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you even still have scars, marks on your arm from the injuries you received at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were beaten to the point where you were beaten to the ground at least ten times prior to your getting on the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell the exact number, but I did fall several times. It could have been ten; it could have been even more, but I did fall to the ground on a number of times, but I did not count.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you finally made it to the truck, you became unconscious for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not completely unconscious; semi-unconscious, dazed, beaten-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have told us about your arrival at Celebici and your having been confined first in Tunnel Number 9. I want to ask you just a couple of questions about that; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From the time you were placed in Tunnel Number 9 until the time you were transferred to Hangar Number 9, I believe it to be your testimony that during that seven day period you were only subjected to one beating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once while being put into the tunnel and then the second time I was brought out and beaten, yes, so in total twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about from the time when you were put in until the time you were taken out, during that seven day period you were taken out and beaten on one occasion; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you say that the way you were all arranged in that tunnel was that you were sitting facing each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that that tunnel is entirely too narrow for two people to sit across from each other and face each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that you probably know the measurements of the tunnel. We were facing each other. So that would mean we were leaning against the walls. We would have our legs pulled up and we would face one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that the situation during the entire time you were in Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time we had to lean against the wall and our knees up, pulled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You described for the -- I want to now go to the time after you went to Hangar 6. You described for the Tribunal yesterday an incident in which your hand was burned with a knife. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you be able to show all of us and show the court the scars on your hand that are left from that burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I perhaps ask your Honours that the ELMO be positioned in such a way that he can put his hand on the ELMO and we can see by that method the scars that remain on his hand. Can you see your monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see your hand on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Have you ever told anyone -- let me do it this way. No. I'll ask this question. Have you ever told anyone that there was a time while you were in Hangar 6 that you reached outside underneath the wall of Hangar 6 and picked grass to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Personally I did not. I said that I ate grass after I would come out, after I would go to the toilet. I could not do it the way you describe it, because I was on the side where there was concrete; in other words, where there was the parking area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention now to the incident you have described regarding the two brothers Dordic. You know the incident that I'm talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The incident you described yesterday involving the sexual matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you've told us yesterday is you don't really remember the guard or guards that were involved in that, and I just want to suggest to you that the guard involved in that was a fellow by the name of Osman Dedic. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday about a detainee by the name of Bosko Samoukovic, and I want to direct your attention now to that situation; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to what it was that caused the death of Mr. Samoukovic and when it was Mr. Samoukovic died, I take it that you would rely on what Dr. Relja might know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My statement is based on personal experience, what I saw with respect to that incident. What I said is what I personally saw, not what other people said or through somebody else's experience. It was my own experience. I had access to -- I personally had access to what was going on, visual access to what was going on at that time regarding Mr. Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm really talking about is after the time that Mr. Samoukovic was removed from Hangar 6 and taken to the infirmary in Building 22. You would have no personal knowledge about what happened after he was removed from Hangar 6, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what happened there. I only know what happened in the hangar and how he was beaten up, how he -- and I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For what happened after he was removed from Hangar 6 and taken to Building 22, you would rely on what Dr. Relja might have said about his condition and how it was that he might have died; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would object to this. This witness doesn't have to rely on anything that anyone else has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I accept that. I think that's a correct objection. The last question I want to ask you, the last area I want to talk to you about, involves the first visit to Celebici of the International Committee of the Red Cross. Do you remember about when that visit was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall the date, but I can say approximately about a month and a half or two after my imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, do you not, that about two weeks prior to that visit Mr. Landzo had left Celebici and was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just remind the court that during the break I will have an opportunity to see the statement this morning and I may have some additional questions I may want to ask the witness after having an opportunity to see that, but other than that I've completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Two questions, your Honour. You reported that Mr. Mucic at some point insulted you. Do you remember any details about what happened or where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During one of the visits to the camp Mucic came in and it was like a review. He started up on the right-hand side. He would talk to somebody. He talked to the ones that he knew, I guess. He knew my brother personally. He came to the place where my brother and I were. He asked about my and his release and he said: "He's a Cetnik. He'll never be released. He'll be killed".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just so I can clarify, was it your brother who asked about your release and was it Mucic who said: "He is a Cetnik. He'll never be released. He'll be killed"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my brother asked. I did not dare ask and I did not want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it Mucic who gave the response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He gave the response and if I can just add, your Honours, in conversation with the witness I found out this and if needed this person is prepared to provide this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, is this clarification arising out of cross-examination or are you bringing in additional material?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it was direct clarification of an issue raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What was the clarification there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The clarification was what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe when Defence Counsel raises a new issue the Prosecution is allowed to ask the circumstances surrounding that. I think this is very fair re-examination, if I am naming it correctly. Let me go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have an objection on the basis that one of the answers which is given at page 32, line 13, appears to indicate that, in fact, this witness is relying on something related to him by somebody completely different: "In conversation with the witness". I have the usual objection that it appears the proper foundation for introducing what appears to be hearsay evidence has not been laid. I invite the Prosecution to do it. If it is unable to do it, I object to the admissibility of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you understood that the additional answer he gave was not an answer which was directed to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may clarify that -- I mean, I have to answer your Honours I don't know. So I will be happy to, as Mr. Greaves has requested, clarify this. Sir, is this something you yourself heard Mr. Mucic say, and, if not, who told you he said it and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean regarding my release or my brother's?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The conversation you indicated where Mr. Mucic said with reference to you that you would not be released for the reasons he gave, did you yourself hear that or did someone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I personally heard that. This happened in the hangar. My brother was lying next to me. I was next to him. He asked for both himself and myself and these were his exact words, that I would never be released because I was a Cetnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, sir: you indicated in cross-examination that in the very first period of time when you were at the camp you received some indication leading you to believe that Rale may have been commander. What could you observe or learn about the role of Rale in Celebici, if any, after that very first period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that at the time when we were brought to Celebici -- this is my personal opinion -- Rale was somebody who was in charge, maybe not the camp commander, but somebody who was in charge, who had a group. I clarified this yesterday. When we were brought off the truck, the first three were beaten, and he said: "Don't beat the people". That's what I tried to use to get off the truck. However, I saw, as I was climbing off the truck, that he was getting into the car and then he left and then I received beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: you have testified about that first -- that very first period. After that very first period, what did you observe or learn about whether or not Rale continued to have any kind of role in the camp, after that first period that you have already testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after transfer to the hangar I did not see Rale and I don't know what his activities were. That means only when I was brought to the Celebici, the first time I was brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness can now stand aside. Do you have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We do have another witness who is here to start. The only thing that I would advise your Honours of is pursuant to a joint request that your Honours had granted I believe some months ago this witness is scheduled for a medical examination. I have been informed that that examination is supposed to take place this afternoon. At least one possibility is that we would take our break now such that the Defence counsel would be able to at least receive a verbal translation of this witness, what was in the book. It is only half a page. Then, if necessary, this witness could be recalled immediately such that his medical examination will not be postponed and so that he can leave as scheduled. That's a suggestion for your Honour, but if you do not want to do that, we have another witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It will be convenient. I think what we will do is we will rise now and come back at 11.45 and then take until 1 o'clock when we will rise for lunch. I am sure you should be able to have the translation done. (11.05 am) (Short break) (11.45 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of the witness. I don't know about any other Defence Counsel, but I have completed my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That's all for the witness. I think we can discharge him, subject to his medical examination. Your next witness then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would now be calling Mr. B. Maybe while he is being -- while the usher is getting him, I can raise another issue just as to scheduling that I have previously discussed with Defence Counsel for Mr. Mucic about the issue of the Prosecution Exhibit I believe 155 and the handwriting. Your Honours had indicated that you would like us to file our submissions by Wednesday. The Prosecution is going to file its submission by Wednesday. Mr. Greaves had indicated that he might now wish to at least briefly review ours before filing his response, a proposal to which we do not have any objection. If I may, I might respectfully suggest to the court and find out if it is acceptable, whether or not if the Prosecution files its response by Wednesday, as directed by the court, if the Defence of Mr. Mucic files their response by either Friday or Monday, and then if there's any argument that your Honours desire, that could be heard immediately upon our resuming court in the beginning of August. That would also give the Prosecution the opportunity to have Mr. Grant Niemann, our lead counsel, present for the arguments at least. That's what we would be requesting. I have talked with Mr. Greaves about this and he's in full agreement with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend speaks for me on this matter and she accurately reflects the conversation we have had. It is, of course, subject to your Honours' decision. If you want to do it in some other way, that's a matter, of course, for your Honours, but we hope that that suggestion will find favour with all of your Honours this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: When we have received your written submissions, then we'll fix an appropriate date when perhaps argument should be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, your clerk has correctly reminded me that I wish to on behalf of the Prosecution to withdraw Mr. B's request for a screen separating him from the accused. He has determined that he no longer believes that is necessary. So we have informed your personnel, but not your Honours. Please excuse us. We now withdraw the request for a separate screen separating the accused. He continues to wish his identity, including his name, face and identifying characteristics, be protected from the media and, in fact, I would just, if I may, inform Defence Counsel that this witness, as well as the next -- not the next witness but the witness after next, Mr. D, are both very, very sensitive about disclosure to the public or media, and so I would just ask that Defence Counsel, if there's any question in their mind about whether or not a question or answer -- that they ask for private session, and I'll be doing the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Invite the witness now. Let's start. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him take the oath. Witness B (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, good morning. Sir, am I correct that you have requested that your name and identity not be released to the public or the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You will thus be known as Mr. B. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you understand if I or anyone else asks you a question and you believe that the answer might tend to reveal your identity, you can request the judges to give your answer in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance I would now like to show you, sir, on a piece of paper a name, and can you confirm that this is, in fact, your name, without saying it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. B, how old are you at the present time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By nationality I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you living in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 I was living in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you mean Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Konjic town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left the town of Konjic on 17th April. I went to a nearby village. The war had started in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were hardly any supplies. I had one and a half year old child. I couldn't find the necessary food for my child, so I went to a village hoping that the supplies would be better there. That was the period when I left Konjic. If you're thinking of all the times that I left Konjic, I left Konjic during my studies, when I went to Sarajevo, but I don't suppose that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So in May and June of 1992 where were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May and June 1992 I was living in the village of Brdjani, near Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when there was military action in Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Military operations occurred in Brdjani. The Muslims attacked our village. I can say that I didn't see the Muslim troops, but when the artillery attack started on the village there was a shower of shells and anti-aircraft grenades and so we all scattered. The attack lasted for maybe two days roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you participate in any defence of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand the question, because nobody took part in the defence of that village, and therefore I didn't either. There was no organised defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you armed during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What did you do during the attack on Brdjani? Can you just briefly describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I ran for my life. That would be my briefest response. If you want me to give you a more detailed answer, I can say that suddenly out of the blue a shower of shells fell on Brdjani. There were bullets flying all over, hitting our houses, and so we all ran for our lives into the nearby woods, and I think that perhaps we were lucky that there were such thick woods in the immediate surroundings, so we managed to escape there and hide.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that forest we managed to reach the village of Bradina. I walked for about two days, I think all of two days, to cover less than 10 km., because the forest was constantly being shelled, hit by grenades and fired upon, so that we could move with difficulty. We went in small groups as we happened to form them, and we somehow reached this village. My estimate is that it was no more than 10 km. away. The village of Bradina at that time had still not been attacked. Before the war the majority population was Serb, so that we thought that we would be safer there. There were some reports that we heard of in Brdjani, even though reports were highly unreliable and there was a lot of misinformation, and this proved to be misinformation, that the women and children of the village of Bradina would be evacuated through the mediation of the Red Cross and they would be 100 per cent safe, and this didn't happen, and of course all of us who had children, we wanted to save them. That's why we all headed for Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was it then approximately, if you know, that the attack on Brdjani happened and you then spent two days going to Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When talking about dates, I mean, I'm not very good at history, and I shall try and be as precise as possible, but please bear with me when dates are involved. I think the attack on Brdjani took place between 10th and 15th May. I'm not quite sure regarding the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: After you went to Bradina, how long did you stay in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Bradina I don't recollect exactly. A few days, maybe five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, when the attack on Brdjani was over, I could climb to a nearby hill from Bradina to see whether Brdjani was still exposed to shelling, and when I saw that calm had returned, I took my wife and child and we returned to our home in Brdjani, and we continued living in our family house in Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened after you returned to Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I returned to Brdjani I stayed to live there in my house. In the village there were very few people left. A lot of people had fled. Some stayed on in Bradina, thinking it was safer. I personally didn't agree with that, because I saw that Bradina really had no defence against the Muslims, that the people were extremely disorganised, even though they had some infantry weapons, but there was no safety there. So I returned to Brdjani and I stayed there until I was imprisoned in the camp. I simply stayed in the village. I didn't move around anywhere except maybe a couple of dozen metres around my house, because it was dangerous anyway to move around.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly what happened such that were then imprisoned in Celebici? Can you please describe to us exactly how that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Bradina fell, not the first or second day, but maybe a certain period of time elapsed and just one man came, a Muslim. I don't know what his official function was. I think he was in the Muslim military police. His surname was Pavo. I have forgotten his first name. I know him -- I knew him very well from before the war. He read out a list of names of all those people who had to report allegedly for an informative interview in the nearby village of Podorasac. Actually the list included the names of all the men, absolutely all the men from the village of Brdjani. Some had stayed behind in Bradina and they were brought with the people from Bradina to the camp, but all the others who were there were on the list; at least I think so. So that as soon as he read out the list the order was that we move immediately. We had absolutely no choice. Because of our families, we had to go to this village of Podorasac, although we presumed roughly what was lying in wait for us and it proved true, because in the village of Podorasac we were --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I ask you: at this time were you told what would happen to you after the informative interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue with what happened when you went to the village of Podorasac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we reached the village of Podorasac, we were ordered to board one or two trucks. The trucks were closed. We still didn't know where we were being taken. Nobody had told us, but after some fifteen or 20 minutes -- I don't know exactly -- we were ordered to get off. We saw where we had come. We had arrived at a former military facility in Celebici, which was later used as a camp for prisoners. We got there. We were ordered to get off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a minute here. Can you tell us, if you know, the approximate date then that you were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just to get an overview, can you just tell us now how long you stayed in Celebici? When was it that you finally left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Celebici in the second half of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going back now to when you arrived at Celebici, do you remember about what time of day it was and do you remember about how many persons were brought to Celebici at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say roughly how many people there were. I think about between 50 and 60 men were brought there. That's my estimate. We were brought there somewhere around midday, around 12 o'clock, maybe 1 in the afternoon. I don't remember exactly, because the man who came and informed us to go to Podorasac, he must have come somewhere around 10.00 in the morning. Then it took us an hour to get to Podorasac, so that must have been 11.00. So it must have been between 12.00 and 1.00 in the afternoon. I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Between the time you were brought to Podorasac and then you were transported to Celebici, during this time, in other words the time before you got to the camp, can you tell us whether or not you were physically mistreated? I am not asking you for details. I am just asking at the time you were arrested or while you were being transported to the camp were you mistreated physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not physically mistreated. I don't know whether other people were, because this was a large group of people, and I couldn't have insight into what happened to each and every one of them. Whether somebody got beaten or not, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going to when you arrived at Celebici, can you please tell us what happened when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the camp we were ordered to get off the trucks and to line up against a wall about 20 metres long, something like that, a concrete wall. I don't know exactly. It was at the very entrance into the camp. Normally everything was done with a lot of curses, threats and other humiliation. We were ordered to empty our pockets, to give whatever we had, belts, laces, watches, money. Everything we owned we had to put next to us. Then we were ordered to form a line and to follow the guards. There were guards accompanying us all the time, and we headed towards a part of the camp. At the time I didn't know where I was going nor where we would be put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a minute here, if I may, sir. Was anything taken from you personally at the entrance, when everyone had to empty their pockets? Was anything of value taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us that had watches, we had to take off our watches. We had to give them whatever we had actually in our pockets. Money, we had to hand over money, though by then already Yugoslav money could not be considered a value at that time. It was simply a pile of paper circulating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was anything of value taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camp I had to surrender my watch and about a month later I had to give my ring, but I gave my ring maybe a month after I had come. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever get either your watch or your ring back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was never returned. Nothing was ever returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you made to say anything when you first arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon our arrival, no. Nobody asked me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue then with what happened after you and the others gave up your valuables.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were ordered to move -- to follow the guard. I was somewhere in the middle of the group. We were brought to a plateau near this wall. It wasn't very far. There was a plateau. Actually there was nothing there except manholes with some installations for fuel or for water. I really don't know. I'm not an expert for these things. These manholes were 2-3 metres deep. It depends. They ordered us to enter those manholes. Some of them were half full of water. In some there was no water. In some there were five men; in others there were ten. We were all forced into these manholes. I can't -- it is difficult for me to say how long we spent in those manholes, because I think one loses all track of time under those circumstances. I thought it was an eternity I had spent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask you: do you know who any of the persons other than the other prisoners who were present at the time that you were -- you and the other prisoners were placed into the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were Muslim guards who were present. The team from the camp, who was working in the camp all the time. So the relationship was between prisoners and guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know the names of anyone from the camp who was present at the time you were put into the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I knew a few people, but I've forgotten the names. I remember certain nicknames. In charge of this team of guards when we were brought to the camp and taken to the manhole, the Commander was Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please go on. While you were in the pit, could you hear -- the manhole, could you hear anything coming from any other manholes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. One could hear the sounds coming from the other manholes. What I was particularly shocked and surprised by, because at that time I didn't know that my father who was in town at the time, who was brought there at the same time as me and put in a manhole with me -- not with me; he was in another manhole. I heard his cries for help. He's a man of 65, 66, and quite sick. I heard his cries that he was choking; he would choke to death while he was in the manhole. Then I recognised that it was my father. I heard somebody opening the manhole next to ours. Soon they opened ours too, ordered us to come out and the first thing I saw was my father, who was sitting next to the neighbouring manhole and he seemed lost. He was hardly -- he was hardly conscious. That was one of the first shocks I experienced upon being brought to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say that your father was in town at the time, what town do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the town of Konjic. I have told you that I was brought from the village of Brdjani where we had a family home, an old family home, but we were living in the town of Konjic and my father was in our apartment in the town of Konjic. Since his name was read out in the list in Brdjani and he was not in the village at the time, he was brought from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now at the time that you were removed from the manhole do you remember anyone from the camp who was present at the time you were removed from the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we were removed we were ordered to form a line again, and I again saw Hazim Delic. I saw Pavo Mucic. He was standing to the left of me. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He had sunglasses on. I remember his presence very well and the other guards were always there. There were plenty of guards always.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At this time when you first got to the camp did you notice anything about Mr. Delic's physical condition at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic at that time was limping on one leg. I cannot remember which leg. He had been hurt, I don't know how. He must have been injured. Some people were saying that he had been wounded. Others said that he got injured when robbing a cafe. I really don't know. Anyway it is a fact that his leg was injured and that he was limping.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened then after you were taken out of the manhole? Where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After being taken out of the manhole we were ordered to follow a path after a guard, following a guard, and there were others, of course, and we were brought in front of a hangar, a military warehouse, a metal structure some 25 metres long and 10-15 metres wide. I don't know exactly. We entered one by one. We were lined up in front and then we were ordered to enter one by one. We were assigned a position where we would sit and that is where we had to sit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe approximately where you sat in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sat very, very close to the door, the entrance to the hangar, on the shorter side, so I was sitting on the width side of the hangar, three or four metres from the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stay in Hangar 6 the entire time you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many prisoners approximately there were in Hangar 6 when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When our group was brought there to the hangar in Celebici, we filled the whole hangar. There wasn't any more room left. We were distributed along the length and width of the hangar and also in the middle some kind of concentric circles were formed. I think there must have been between 350 and 400 men. It's impossible for me to give the exact figure because neither did I dare, nor did I have the possibility to count, nor did it occur to me to count the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe the living conditions in Hangar 6, the food, the toilet facilities, water? Can you just please describe the living conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In detail or just one word? Horror. Or are you interested in more?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In detail, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Horror is a mild word for this. In the camp there was dirt, filth, infectious skin diseases. We didn't wash for a month. In the camp we had lice. As for food, we got one piece -- a thin piece of bread a day, but there were periods where we didn't get even that. We drink water, industrial water that was given to us in bottles. It was taken from the hydrants, from these devices for fire-fighting devices, so that frequently people had intestinal troubles and other problems probably due to the water and to the general conditions in the camp. They were inhuman, absolutely inhuman conditions. There was terrible hunger. We didn't have anything to eat and we were not allowed to receive food. It was only after the Red Cross came to visit that we were allowed to receive food from people outside. So that I can say that almost throughout my stay in the camp I had 90 kilos before the war. When I came out I weighed some 50 kilos and that applied to all of us. We were living corpses. When people got up, we were ordered to sit, and when we were allowed to get up to go to the toilet or if the guards closed the doors and one could get up just to stretch, many people would faint. They were so exhausted, many.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were you sometimes allowed out of Hangar 6 to perform certain duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not just me, but there were other prisoners too who went out of the hangar, because all the chores that needed to be done in the camp, this military facility was not just a camp; it was a warehouse for armaments and ammunition for the Muslim army. It was like a barracks for a time for the Muslim army. People came for training or for some kind of gatherings. I don't know. I have no idea of. I know there was another building full of Muslim troops. There were duties. So I went out frequently to do things, like unloading weapons or unloading food or washing somebody's car. People often came for the prisoners to wash their cars or to do some other cleaning duty, moving things from one place to another. There were often such duties to perform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was it who usually asked you to perform these duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually a guard would come who was on duty. He would probably be given orders to collect so many prisoners to do a certain task, and sometimes they would ask whether anybody wants to work. Another time he would say: "The first five from this row" or "another five from this row". There were various ways in which they selected prisoners for work. Sometimes you would go out just to have a chance to wash your hands or wash up after completing this duty. Some people even volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there someone present at the camp named Mr. Ivica Buric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Ivica Buric was in the camp. He was actually the driver of Pavo Mucic. He was the driver in the camp. He also drove for other purposes, not just for Pavo, probably to get certain supplies or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Buric from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Buric several times before the war. I didn't know him well, but I had excellent relationships with his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there some occasions where Mr. Buric called you out or requested that you be called out to perform certain tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It happened quite often. Again I can't say how many times, but usually, as this was in my interest, he would ask me to wash his car, because in that way I myself could keep clean. On a number of occasions he would offer me food. That was one of the ways for him to be able to do it. Sometimes when he was forced to act as a guard in place of somebody, he would take me out because the temperature in the hangar was unbearable. It was extremely high in the summer. We were there in the summer, when for two or three months there wasn't a drop of rain. So you can imagine what it was like under a steel roof, in a steel structure. So it was almost a pleasure to be taken out to do anything -- except for beating, of course -- and he would take me out and we would talk when he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During your conversations with Mr. Buric did he ever provide you information concerning who he worked for or how the camp structure was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spoke about everything. We would touch all kinds of subjects. Throughout that time I had the impression that he was almost apologising, that he found it hard why these things were happening, why Serbs and Croats were fighting one another. He couldn't accept that. He said he was horrified by what the Muslims were doing in the camp to the Serbs, both the male and female prisoners, and I think that he and Pavo were the only Croats there, at least during my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Buric ever indicate to you that he had talked with anyone about the fact that you would or would not be mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, it's natural when you get into some kind of trouble to try and find a way out in some possible way, so I asked Buric whether he could help me somehow, because I saw that people were getting killed, beaten up, and he told me -- he promised that he would talk to Pavo to try and protect me, so that nothing terrible should happen to me, and on one occasion he even told me that Pavo had told him to tell me not to worry, that nothing terrible would happen to me. Of course, everything was terrible, but when I say something terrible, I'm thinking of not getting killed in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about exactly -- well, do you remember anything about when these conversations were with Mr. Buric? Were they the entire time you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I don't count the first five or six days, but after those five or six days throughout my stay in the camp, sometimes twice a day he would call me. Sometimes he wasn't there for a day or two, but we had contact very frequently throughout my stay in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were at the camp, how frequently would you yourself see Mr. Mucic present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to tell precisely how often and on what occasions, but on average about twice a month. That would mean not too often. The first meeting was immediately upon my arrival and then the next one, ten days later. Then there was a period of time when I wouldn't see him. Maybe some others did see him, because, as I said, I did not stay in this hangar all the time. I often did something, worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So on those occasions when you did see Mr. Mucic, where would it be? Would it be inside the hangar or outside the hangar? Can you just tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part it was in the hangar. Pavo Mucic would come escorted by some guards, and would always order them to stay at the door to watch us. He would go from one prisoner to the next and in this way he would actually review all the prisoners. He would ask some questions of someone and some he would just pass by. Usually the questions were: "What did you have? What kind of weapons did you have?" At least that's what he asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic have an office at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How do you know that he had an office at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I was taken with another prisoner to clean in this part where these offices were. There was also a room where people ate and also I think there was a dormitory. Delic had an office there.
