Do you recall testifying about that on direct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you see the people milling around that were not part of the guard force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see them. I must tell you that at that time I had the impression that I shouldn't turn around much and look around. That was the impression that I had, so that I could only see the guards, maybe not even all the guards. I would see somebody who was in front of me or just in my line of vision. I couldn't see the guards behind me and I didn't turn around much and look around whether there were other people there, and in this kind of a situation it's a bit unnatural to sort of wander around and look at the landscape or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand. Sir, thank you very much. Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would just like to inform the Registrar, please, that I will need those three photographs of the people from Belgrade in a few moments also. I don't know the numbers of those. Thank you. May it please the court? Thank you. Good afternoon, Witness B. My name is Cynthia McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm defence attorney for Mr. Esad Landzo. I know that the Prosecutor has already discussed this with you, but one of the things that I would like to ask you to agree with me on this afternoon is when you are giving evidence in the courtroom that you only testify or talk about things that you personally experienced or that you personally heard or that you personally witnessed. Do we have an agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that you visited with the Prosecutor -- you said Mr. -- I can't pronounce his name either -- Mr. Hortemo -- is that his name -- with the Prosecutor's Office in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you granted him an interview at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution some time between that point and now told you that we of the defence would like a chance to interview and talk to you about your experiences at Celebici also, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you responded to them that you did not want to discuss that with us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you decided that you would not give us the same courtesy that you gave the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know why I would -- I had a special courtesy for the Prosecution. I had no time to talk to anybody from the Defence and I didn't think that it was necessary. I was given a choice and if you are given a choice, you take the option that you use more. I didn't ever feel that this was my obligation, because that was not how it was put to me. Since I have agreed to -- since I agreed to come here, I knew that I would accept, as they call it, the rules of the game and talk to everyone, but I was given a choice to talk to you or not and then I chose not to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. We respect your choice also. Thank you. You stated earlier that, of course, you made a statement to the Office of the Prosecution and you said you also spoke to the Serbian Women's Caucus and you also mentioned something about a tourist travel agency. Can you tell us what kind of statement you might have made to a tourist travel agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously either it was misinterpreted or it was maybe misunderstood. When your colleague asked me before about the circumstances under which I gave a statement, I was very clear. There was no organisation of Serbian Women that I gave this statement to. I gave this statement exclusively to Mr. Hortemo in the present of his interpreter -- I mean his interpreter -- yes, in the presence of his interpreter, and it seemed to me at that time that I did not need to answer who organised this, and I said: "Well, it could have been organised even by a tourist travel agency". Obviously I did not give any statements to a tourist travel agency, because I said already that I had not given any statements to anyone except to the representatives of this Tribunal, provided that Mr. Hortemo is or was a representative of this Tribunal. So that was what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time I would like to ask, with the assistance of the usher, that these three photographs be shown to Mr. B, please, and just for the record, could I have what the numbers of those three photographs are?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 5/2, 6/2 and 7/2 exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we start with the first photograph? Can we put it on the ELMO also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How do you identify these numbers to correspond with what he has?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will have to ask the usher to assist me with that. Thank you. Mr. Usher, can you tell us the number of the photograph that you are putting on the ELMO first, please? THE USHER: D6/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. B, can you tell me if you have ever seen this woman before, if you recognise this woman, not from what's on the monitor now. If we could just have it focused a second. Thank you. Have you ever seen that woman before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've not. I think I have not seen her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we go on to the next photograph, please? THE USHER: D5/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This photograph is D5/2 and, Mr. B, can you look at this photograph and tell me if you have ever seen this person before and if you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And can you tell us who he is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Dr. Milivoy -- it is even written down there. There is a caption down there with his name. Otherwise I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You do know him because you saw him in Belgrade; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you know him as the President of the Association of Detainees in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is true that at some point this person examined you in Belgrade, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When he examined you, did you give a statement to him about your experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When he examined you in Belgrade, did he take X-rays of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember. I really can't remember whether he took X-rays or not. I did have an examination, but I don't know that any -- whether any X-rays were included in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So if there were X-rays, he didn't give them to you, did he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That's a very awkward question. He didn't know whether there were X-rays so the condition of whether if there were is a very --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'll move on, your Honour. Do you remember whether you had any urine samples taken and any reports done of your urine as part of your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can't remember. I can tell you the examination took place maybe five years ago and in that period things were happening to me, such big things and such big changes in my life, that I had to fight for my existence, for my survival. There was the question of moving from Belgrade and things like that. So I really can't remember these details from a medical examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you can't remember what occurred at the medical examination, but you do remember that you did not make a statement about your experiences at Celebici to this gentleman, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had certain difficulties in the area of my back and it's quite possible that he must have asked me what happened. "Did you fall? Is it from a blow?", or things like that. I don't know what the exact term is in medicine when a doctor wants to find out how an injury or a medical problem started. So it's quite possible for a doctor to ask you: "Did you fall or did somebody hit you?", so as to know how to treat you. He must know the origin of your injury and I may have told him that I was detained in a camp. I find it difficult to recall the exact wording of what I said, but I'm saying that it's quite probable that he did ask me this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were aware that this doctor was also associated with the Association of Detainees in Belgrade, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know that such an association existed in Belgrade, nor was I ever a member of that association, nor -- I got the address of Dr. Bjelica from another detainee, a relative of mine, and the first few days when we arrived to Serbia nobody reported, because we were afraid of mobilisation and who knows what else could happen. Later on our fears proved to be unfounded, so we had no medical documents, no documents at all, and I learned that this man was a highly humane one, that he would examine us without any payment and we needed this examination without having to pay for it. I hadn't known him from before, nor was I aware that he was a member of any association, nor did I know his surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say that none of you reported when you first arrived in Belgrade, do you mean that none of you reported to this doctor for an examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Please be more precise if you are asking me things like that. I never said that nobody reported to the authorities when they came to Belgrade or somewhere else in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I didn't report immediately to the authorities. When I learned that one could do so without any consequences, I did, but a couple of days went by before we reported to the authorities, before we registered. I did later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just realised that I'm being inconsiderate to the usher. Would you please remove that photograph and show him the third one so we can finish with the photographs? That would be? THE USHER: D7/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: D7/2. Do you recognise this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I would just like the record to reflect that the only one he recognised was D5/2; is that correct? THE USHER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So when you got to Belgrade, you did not ask the Association of Detainees for any assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe earlier you had stated that you were not interested in politics at all, but as an economist, you know for a fact that economics and politics are intrinsically intertwined, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, but maybe I need to expand a little on my answer. Politics and economics -- in the firm I was working in, I dealt with the domestic market. Politics is necessary for economies dealing with export and import so as to know what kind of a political situation is in a particular country, whether it is appropriate for investment, whether capital was fleeing from that country and so on. I was saying that politics was not my preoccupation, but if you insist, it is normal that no-one can 100 per cent isolate himself from politics. If you have ears and eyes you have to see or hear things in the papers, on television. You have to have some kind of knowledge about it, but that was not my occupation, nor was it my preoccupation or my interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you did testify that you were aware that the political situation basically had rendered the Yugoslav money worthless; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe in your testimony earlier also you had testified that the Muslim troops attacked Brdjani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you were listening carefully to my answers, I said that I fled from the village of Brdjani as soon as this shower of shells started falling. I don't know exactly what firearms were being used, was it anti-aircraft machine guns or something like that. I didn't see Muslim troops entering the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you did know -- you know now that it was not Muslim troops; it was a combined forces of HVO, HOS and TO forces, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object or at least get Defence Counsel to withdraw her previous instruction that this witness should only testify about what he himself observed, since he has already stated he himself did not observe this. If she wants to ask him about hearsay, I don't object, but I just think we should be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I will ask him if he knows from his studies since that time whether it was a combined force.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then I would only ask for clarification of the word "studies", your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'll move on. I really don't think it's that important at this point. Thank you. You also claimed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a very good game.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I can give occasionally. The Muslim military police you said came to arrest you on the second half of June. Isn't that true? Didn't you say it was the Muslim military police? That's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't recall saying that the Muslim police came to arrest me on 2nd June. If you can explain a little, when did I make the statement on 2nd June?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In your direct testimony earlier you stated in the second half of June -- you couldn't remember the exact day -- that the Muslim military police came to Brdjani and read out a list of 50 to 60 men from Brdjani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Originally the translation I got was "2nd June", not "the second half of June". In the second half of June I assume he was working for the Muslim military police, Mr. Spago. I have just remembered his first name. I think it was Ferid. He read out a list, but please don't insist on the number. My estimate was that it was between 50 and 60 men. There may have been fewer or more than that. That was my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My specific point of interest is that there was not really any Muslim military police; that that was a combined force also, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very uncertain about military terminology. For me a force means several people. This was one individual, a member of the Muslim military police. I'm sorry I'm using the term "Muslim military police". Maybe at that time they called themselves "Territorial Defence" and later became the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know exactly, but anyway I'm saying it so that you know who I mean. It was this one man, Ferid Spago. Maybe someone else went to the other end of the village. Mountain villages consist of several hamlets with quite isolated homes and households. I don't know whether someone else went to a different part of the village. All I remember is Ferid Spago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think what counsel is trying to explain to you is that there is no such organisation known as the Muslim military police. That's what she's saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you know of any such organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew a man who told me. I said I was using the term "Muslim" to indicate that it was not a Serbian. This may not be an organisation, but a part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was the military police. I suppose there is a military police in any country in the world, and I just wanted to say that one member of that section came and read out this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move back to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. May I just add, I was not saying a paramilitary organisation had come that called itself the military police or any such separate group that had the words "military police" in its name. I have never implied that this was a separate organisation, just as a part of a force.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're all clear on that now. Thank you. I want to move back to -- Madame Residovic, who is the attorney for Mr. Delalic, had shown a video earlier today. In that video you did recognise that as Konjic and you did recognise that as the Serbian Orthodox Church of some sort. Can you tell me: do you recognise that line of people as a line of persons in Konjic waiting to receive food rations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must first say that my impression was that it was Konjic. After all, there are many towns that have a river and lots of greenery along the banks. Since this is a trial about Celebici and Konjic, it's normal that I should assume that it was Konjic and it resembles Konjic. I also assume that it is the Orthodox Church, and what those people were waiting for in the line and what they were carrying in the bags I really can't tell. Though I come from Konjic and I lived a long time there, I didn't recognise anyone in that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Even though you didn't recognise anyone in that line, you don't recognise that that was a line of people needing to receive food in Konjic; is that what you are testifying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you think he should come to such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I was just asking if he did recognise it as a food line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How could he?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: How could he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there anything written in the video to indicate that there was such a food line?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It looked like a food line to me, but maybe it doesn't look like a food line to him. That is all I'm trying to elicit. If it doesn't look like a food line to him, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So many people may draw different conclusions from such a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It could have been for paper and pencils. Okay. Thank you. You did testify that even for the last year that food supplies were in short supply in Konjic, didn't you? I know you testified about baby food, but there were shortages of other food in Konjic in 1992, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, about other supplies I don't know. I know that very frequently I would bring various baby foods from Sarajevo, which doesn't mean to say that you could never find it in Konjic, but it was easier to find it in Sarajevo, as the centre of the Republic, which was far better supplied, than in a relatively small town like Konjic. It was my mother who usually went to the market, my wife. They did the shopping, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Since you lived in Konjic and you worked in Sarajevo, were you aware that in the month of April there were some maybe 20,000 refugees that were coming through Konjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You had testified earlier today about certain injuries to a Nedeljko Draganic, a Dusko Bendzo and a few other persons that you mentioned. Just for clarification, I would like to say that you maybe saw the injuries of these people, but you didn't see what actually happened to them outside the hangar, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stated very clearly today which injuries of which people and which tortures I eyewitnessed. After that I said what kind of injuries I saw, and I can add to that that I really did see those injuries, but I didn't see the moments when those burns were inflicted. I did see other things. Maybe, if necessary, I can clarify further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you just clarified it. Thank you very much. I appreciate that. I also wanted to bring to your attention to -- I wanted to ask if you were aware of an incident that happened on July 12th, 1992, where a group of military police were murdered in an area called Repovci, I think. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't recall the date, but it was somewhere around then, and I had heard that a group of military policemen had got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you knew a few of those military policemen from Konjic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps one might say that I knew a couple, maybe two of them. I have never learned of all the names of the people who were killed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you remember, those were considered very brutal murders, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not on the spot, nor did I have too much information, nor did I dare at the time enquire. So I just knew that an incident had occurred, that some people had got killed. I know I knew one personally. I think I knew another. I'm not quite sure, but I know absolutely no details. I don't know who conducted the investigation, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified earlier that occasionally a guard would come into Hangar 6. He had probably been given orders to pick a few of the detainees in there and take them out to work. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Even though you were merely an exchange operator in your service in the JNA, from your military experience you know that as a rule the guards follow orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was organised, whether in their army somebody follows orders or acts on his own initiative. If that is your assumption, you may be right. That's all I can say. I'm not sure at all what the method of command in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is. Maybe I shouldn't even have made that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You are aware that some time before the International Red Cross came to visit you in August that Mr. Landzo left Celebici, didn't he? He was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know the exact date when Mr. Landzo left Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You also before the war knew a gentleman -- and I don't want to repeat his surname here in open court -- but you knew a gentleman named Miro, who was a restaurant owner in Konjic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not "Miro". That was just the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. I was just using his nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you avoided the surname, the name is not correct either. It is a nickname. I want to make sure that we have the same person in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think it is a person that you were aware that Mr. Landzo worked for before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned later. I must have seen Landzo in that restaurant a couple of times without paying any attention to him at the time, but this was a very, very good friend of mine, Mr. Miro, so that it is most probable that that is where I saw Landzo. I learned only later that he had worked there, because, you know, if you go to a restaurant, if you see someone in a restaurant, it need not necessarily mean that he's working there. I didn't pay any attention to what capacity -- to the capacity in which he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But while you were in Celebici, you found out that Mr. Landzo was also friends with Miro, and so you two became semi-friends. He never harmed you in Celebici, did he, Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Mr. Landzo never did anything wrong to me. I didn't say that he did. It is not Mr. Landzo's fault that I came to Celebici. He didn't bring me there. I'm just saying what I saw or heard. It is quite correct that he did not inflict any harm on me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you one final question. It's true that, at the risk of himself being chastised or getting in trouble, Mr. Landzo allowed your wife to come visit with you in his dug-out while you were in Celebici, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just one question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the persons you saw who were burned and otherwise had injuries from burns or heated instruments, can you just please clarify which incidents or which persons of what you have already testified to did you yourself see what happened as it happened and which you saw the injuries afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The incidents that I personally eyewitnessed was the one with the ear of one of the prisoners with the hot red pincers; then wrapping a fuse around the body of one of the brothers; frequent kicking of people while they were doing push-ups. What else did I mention? As for burns, I didn't see the moment when the burns were inflicted. I just saw those injuries, but not the moment when they were done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that was the only question I had for re-examination. I will just inform your Honours that the Translation Section has provided me with corrected translations, in which the word "her" has been switched to "his". I have extra copies for Defence Counsel. I also believe in the first sentence instead of saying: "After interrogating the individual whose name appears below ..." they have changed it to say: "After interviewing the below-mentioned individual ...". Those are the only changes. I have extra copies and I would submit them as corrected translations for the exhibit. The exhibit hasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The most offending aspect I think -- this is the masculine being the feminine -- has been changed, I suppose. I think this is the end of this witness' examination. Therefore he is discharged. The Trial Chamber will rise now and reassemble tomorrow morning at 10.00. (5.30 pm)
